entities.name: José Longinos Ellauri
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
José Longinos Ellauri Fernández (1789–1867) emerged as a foundational architect of the nascent Uruguayan state in the tumultuous wake of South American independence. A jurist, politician, and intellectual, Ellauri played a pivotal role in shaping the constitutional framework and early diplomatic relations of the Oriental Republic of Uruguay during a period marked by intense regional rivalries between the Argentine Confederation and the Empire of Brazil. His contributions to the General Constituent and Legislative Assembly from 1828 to 1830 established him as a key proponent of liberal constitutionalism and a central figure in the institutionalization of the young nation, steering it away from the caudillo-dominated politics of its neighbors.

Born in Montevideo, then part of the Spanish Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, Ellauri initially pursued legal studies, grounding him in the principles that would later define his political career. He actively participated in the independence movement, notably joining the *Cabildo Abierto* of 1810 in support of the May Revolution. Following the Portuguese-Brazilian occupation of the Banda Oriental in the 1820s, he endured exile in Brazil. Upon his return after the Cisplatine War and the Preliminary Peace Convention of 1828, Ellauri was elected to the General Constituent and Legislative Assembly, where he was instrumental in drafting and signing Uruguay's first constitution in 1830. He subsequently served multiple terms as Minister of Finance and Minister of Foreign Affairs under early presidents, helping to stabilize the national economy and forge crucial international alliances.

entities.summary:
José Longinos Ellauri Fernández (1789–1867) stands as a pivotal figure in the foundational era of the Oriental Republic of Uruguay, a nation emerging from the tumultuous processes of South American independence. Born in Montevideo on March 14, 1789, Ellauri dedicated his extensive career to shaping the legal and political institutions of the nascent state, navigating its complex transition from Spanish colonial rule and subsequent regional conflicts. His significance lies in his unwavering commitment to constitutionalism and the rule of law during a period marked by profound instability, making him a central architect of Uruguay's early republican framework.

Ellauri’s contributions were multifaceted and instrumental. He served as a key delegate to the 1828 Constituent Assembly, which drafted Uruguay's first constitution, a document critical for establishing national sovereignty. Following its ratification, he became the first President of the Senate in 1830, occupying a crucial role in the initial functioning of the legislative branch. His diplomatic acumen was also widely recognized; he represented Uruguay in Brazil (1840-1843) and later in Argentina during the tumultuous Great War (1843-1851), negotiating crucial agreements that sought to secure the nation's fragile independence and territorial integrity. Perhaps his most enduring legacy, however, was his leadership in the commission that drafted the Uruguayan Civil Code, promulgated posthumously in 1868, which provided the bedrock for the nation's private law.
